verdicts.claim: A checkpoint copies committed content from the WAL file back into the database file. The writer rewinds the WAL to its start only after
verdicts.evidence: wal.html 2.2: 'if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning'

verdicts.claim: By default SQLite auto-checkpoints on the COMMIT that makes the WAL 1000 pages or more (about 4 MB). It also checkpoints when the last
verdicts.evidence: wal.html 3.1: 'checkpoint whenever a COMMIT occurs that causes the WAL file to be 1000 pages or more in size, or when the last database connection on a database file closes'; section 6 'about 4MB'; SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT named

verdicts.claim: Automatic checkpoints are always PASSIVE. sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() is also PASSIVE, and PASSIVE is the default checkpoint style.
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'The default checkpoint style is PASSIVE ... All checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and by the automatic checkpoint mechanism are PASSIVE'

verdicts.claim: PASSIVE copies as many frames as it can without waiting for readers or writers. It can leave the checkpoint unfinished. It never invokes
verdicts.evidence: C API: 'The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode ... passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished'

verdicts.claim: FULL waits, invoking the busy handler, until no writer is active and all readers use the most recent snapshot. ... blocks new writers, but not new readers
verdicts.evidence: C API: 'This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded'

verdicts.claim: RESTART does what FULL does. It then waits, invoking the busy handler, until all readers use only the database file.
verdicts.evidence: C API: 'blocks (calls the busy-handler callback) until all readers are reading from the database file only. This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning'

verdicts.claim: TRUNCATE does what RESTART does. Before a successful return it also truncates the WAL file to zero bytes.
verdicts.evidence: C API: 'also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return'

verdicts.claim: A default checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file ... keeps its high-water size unless journal_size_limit is set.
verdicts.evidence: wal.html 6: 'The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set)'

verdicts.claim: A checkpoint copies WAL content only up to the end mark of each active reader ... A long read transaction therefore prevents checkpoint
verdicts.evidence: wal.html 2.2: 'must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader ... a long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress'

verdicts.claim: Checkpoints are mutually exclusive across processes. If another process is already running a checkpoint, the call fails with SQLITE_BUSY
verdicts.evidence: C API: 'If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked'

verdicts.claim: A checkpoint syncs in a fixed order. The WAL is synced before its content moves into the database, and the database file is synced
verdicts.evidence: wal.html 2.3: 'The WAL must be synced ... prior to moving content ... and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL'; C API PASSIVE 'sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed'

verdicts.claim: By default, the thread that makes the COMMIT that crosses the threshold runs that checkpoint itself. That COMMIT is slow while most
verdicts.evidence: wal.html 2.3: 'run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit ... an occasional COMMIT ... to be much slower'

verdicts.claim: PRAGMA wal_checkpoint and PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(MODE) ... The no-argument form equals sqlite3_wal_checkpoint(). The argument form
verdicts.evidence: pragma.html: 'Invoking this pragma without an argument is equivalent to calling the sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() C interface. Invoking this pragma with an argument is equivalent to ... sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2()'

verdicts.claim: PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint=N sets the auto-checkpoint threshold in pages. A value of zero or less turns auto-checkpointing off.
verdicts.evidence: pragma.html: 'Setting the auto-checkpoint size to zero or a negative value turns auto-checkpointing off. This pragma is a wrapper around the sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() C interface'

verdicts.claim: sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() writes two counts ... Both are -1 on error or when the database is not in WAL mode. After a successful TRUNCATE both are 0.
verdicts.evidence: C API: '-1 if the checkpoint could not run because of an error or because the database is not in WAL mode ... both *pnLog and *pnCkpt will be set to zero'

verdicts.claim: PRAGMA journal_size_limit=N makes SQLite truncate a WAL file larger than N bytes back to N, checked at each commit and WAL reset. The default is -1
verdicts.evidence: pragma.html: 'Each time a transaction is committed or a WAL file resets ... truncated to the limit ... The default journal size limit is -1 (no limit) ... set the journal_size_limit to zero' for minimum

verdicts.claim: The SQLite docs say the 1000-page default seems to work well in test applications on workstations, and other strategies may suit
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'this strategy seems to work well in test applications on workstations, but other strategies might work better on different platforms or for different workloads'

verdicts.claim: Syncthing runs a timer-based checkpointer but leaves auto-checkpoints on, and its authors say the two contend.
verdicts.evidence: Syncthing: 'our application level checkpointer is timer based ... We don't disable the auto checkpoint functionality ... we're blocking our own checkpointer'

verdicts.claim: If at least one reader is always active, no checkpoint can complete, and the WAL grows without bound. A Syncthing thread posted 2026-02-06
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound'; Syncthing post dated February 6, 2026

verdicts.claim: A forced TRUNCATE waits for all active readers and writers to finish before it truncates the WAL. Litestream says this can block
verdicts.evidence: Litestream: 'waits for both all active readers AND writers to complete before truncating the WAL. Long-lived read transactions will cause extended blocking periods'

verdicts.claim: The WAL-reset bug ... likely present in every release from 3.7.0 (2010-07-21) through 3.51.2 (2026-01-09). It is fixed in 3.51.3 (2026-03-13)
verdicts.evidence: wal.html 11: 'likely present in all version of SQLite from 3.7.0 (2010-07-21) through 3.51.2 (2026-01-09). It is fixed in version 3.51.3 (2026-03-13) ... 3.44.6 and 3.50.7'; release log: 'Fix the WAL-reset database corruption bug'

verdicts.claim: The WAL-reset bug needs two or more connections, in separate threads or processes, that write or checkpoint at the same instant.
verdicts.evidence: wal.html 11/11.1: two or more connections 'attempt to write or checkpoint at the same instant'; steps 1-7 match (third checkpoint skips part of step-3 transaction)

verdicts.claim: SQLite says the bug's occurrence rate appears to be at or below the rate of SSD malfunctions or cosmic-ray hits ... Canonical ... very low
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'less than or equal to the expected occurrence rate of SSD malfunctions and/or cosmic-ray hits'; Canonical: 'its real-world impact (which is very low)'

verdicts.claim: Disagreement: wal.html says the WAL-reset bug was found and fixed on 2026-03-03. Canonical says SQLite disclosed the bug ... March 5, 2026
verdicts.evidence: wal.html: 'On 2026-03-03, one of the SQLite developers (Dan) found and fixed a bug'; Canonical: 'On March 5, 2026 SQLite disclosed the bug and published a fix'
